extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and practitioners interested in the theory of humor, literary critics, playwrights and comedic writers studying the mechanics of the comic
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying theoretical criteria for what makes something comic (types of absurdity, logical inversions, dream-logic, social function of laughter) as described in a philosophical/critical essay on laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional language transplanted to ordinary life
rubrics_metrics.description: The ludicrous arises when a professional strategy or specialised mode of expression is applied to the everyday affairs of life (e.g., translating scientific or gambling terms into ordinary speech).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay notes this form of comic is sometimes coarse but may be refined when it reveals a peculiarity of character in addition to a professional habit. Examples: Regnard's Joueur (gambling terms used for people: 'Hector', 'Pallas') and Molière's Femmes savantes (scientific ideas rendered as feminine sensibility: 'Epicure me plait', 'J'aime les tourbillons'). Use of technical vocabulary or modes of thought in inappropriate social contexts produces humour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contrast of professional logic versus universal logic
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain ways of reasoning valid within a specialised circle (professional logic) but untrue or inappropriate for the general public produce comic effects by contrast with universal/common-sense logic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The comic can exploit the clash between a particular, circumscribed reasoning and the broader, expected reasoning of ordinary life; emphasise the mismatch between locally-valid inferences and general common-sense conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic absurdity is a particular, not general, absurdity (privileged recollection dominating perception)
rubrics_metrics.description: Absurdity in the comic is not 'absurdity in general' but a definite inversion of common sense: an idea or privileged recollection in the mind forces perception to conform to itself (e.g., Don Quixote seeing giants where others see windmills).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This criterion stresses that comic effects come from a mind imposing an idea onto the world rather than adapting ideas to facts. The absurdity is specific — a particular inversion where imagination dominates perception — and the effect depends on that peculiar causal relation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rigidity/automatism: following one idea obstinately
rubrics_metrics.description: Comic characters err through obstinacy, absentmindedness or automatism — they 'follow up his one idea' and continually recur to it despite interruptions, progressively failing to adapt to changing circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many comic scenes reduce to a character repeatedly pursuing a single idea; the humour arises from the stubborn refusal to adjust. Molière's characters often exemplify this type. Look for repetitive single-minded behavior as a source of laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dream-logic: relaxed, counterfeit reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: The logic of the comic often mirrors dream-logic: reasonings that are false but resemble those one might accept in a dream — abridged or counterfeit reasoning that lacks intellectual tension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect partially-formed chains of thought, beginnings and ends without full middle steps, surface connections that permit puns or wordplay. This relaxation of reasoning produces relief from intellectual effort and is central to many witticisms and comic sequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Play upon words arising from superficial idea-relations
rubrics_metrics.description: As relations between ideas become more superficial, comic play evolves from ideas to words — the meaning of words is disregarded and sound or superficial resemblance predominates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include scenes where characters repeat or distort whispered words into nonsense (compared to dream-speech). Use of homophony, puns, or meaningless repetition exemplifies this mode.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic obsessions and repetition (dream-like recurrence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Repetitive images or refrains that recur with slight changes (as in dreams) can produce comic effects; repetition confers a comic persistence and varied apparent meanings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for motifs or refrains that repeat across scenes or verses (e.g., the burden of a song) and derive humour from the same element being reinterpreted each time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crescendo toward absurdity
rubrics_metrics.description: Comic sequences may exhibit a 'crescendo' — a progression of concessions or absurdities that grow more pronounced until a crowning, outrageous absurdity is reached.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The mechanism relies on incremental escalation (first concession, then another, then a more serious one). Molière's Monsieur de Pourceaugnac and Le Bourgeois gentilhomme are cited as paradigms where the play begins reasonably and devolves into increasing extravagance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fusion/confusion of identities (double self)
rubrics_metrics.description: A dream-like fusion where a person is simultaneously himself and not himself or where two persons merge into one produces a special comic confusion (e.g., the Mark Twain interviewer dialogue where the speaker alternates narrative perspectives).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This phenomenon creates comic effects when a speaker slips between first- and third-person positions or treats himself as both agent and observer; the oddity derives from the split self familiar from dreams.

rubrics_metrics.name: Initial sympathetic relaxation (invitation to 'join the game')
rubrics_metrics.description: At first the audience may sympathise with the comic character, momentarily adopting their gestures and words — a brief relaxation or playfulness that invites the audience to share the amusement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This fleeting sympathy explains why the comic often feels pleasurable initially: the audience temporarily 'takes it easy' with the character, joining the game before the corrective aspect asserts itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laughter as corrective/social punishment (humiliation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter functions as a social corrective: it humiliates and intimidates the person laughed at, responding to impertinences with an even greater impertinence; its object is to check failings and enforce social norms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a functionalist criterion: comic effects are evaluated by their capacity to mark and punish social deviation. The essay emphasises the punitive, not benevolent, nature of laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spontaneity and potential injustice of laughter
rubrics_metrics.description: Because laughter is an automatic, natural mechanism rather than the product of reflection, it often fails to 'hit the mark' — it may punish the innocent and spare the guilty, aiming at a general corrective effect rather than case-by-case justice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing the ethics or social acceptability of laughter, consider its spontaneous, indiscriminate operation and the resulting unfairness in particular instances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Element of spite/mischief and ego in the laugher
rubrics_metrics.description: Even in well-intentioned laughter there exists a spark of spitefulness or mischief and an expression of egoism — the laugher feels superior, treating the laughed-at as a marionette.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The critic should note the psychological disposition of the laugher: conceit and a tendency toward pessimism underpin much laughter; analysing comic scenes includes examining the laugher's stance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laughter as surface phenomenon reflecting social disturbances (the 'froth' metaphor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter indicates a slight, surface-level revolt in social life — like sea-foam on otherwise peaceful depths — sparkling and gay outwardly but leaving a bitter aftertaste; it reveals and emphasises social undulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this metaphor to evaluate comic material's social role: does the humour merely skim the social surface, producing transient sparkle with an ultimately bitter or corrective intent? Consider the depth (or shallowness) of the comic effect.
